MK: We and our patients are harmed by the air pollution from this outdated coal power plant. We are seeing more respiratory and cardiovascular illness related to poor air quality. Additionally, this plant and others in Illinois are major sources of greenhouse gases. Climate change is worsening the health of people in Waukegan now and the problem is growing.

The pollution emitted from the Waukegan Generating Station increases asthma, bronchitis, allergies, heart attacks, and other respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses. These are terrible illnesses for many people that cannot be fully remedied by medication. The community is suffering from excess deaths, hospital admissions and emergency room visits, lost workdays, and reduced school attendance. In fact, these conditions are contributing to more COVID-19 illness, hospitalizations, and deaths in Waukegan.

As for the coal plants’ contributions to climate change due to its emissions, our patients are vulnerable to increasing heat stress which is especially dangerous for the elderly, pregnant women, and infants. Many people in the community live in poverty without affordable access to air conditioning. Their housing is often in areas that turn into urban heat islands on hot days and do not cool off at night.
Moreover, the Waukegan coal power plant is polluting the groundwater and soil. Toxins from burning coal like mercury are damaging our patients’ brains and other organs.
Closing the Waukegan coal plant will improve air quality in the area. Closing all coal and natural gas power plants in Illinois will help limit heat waves and flooding from extreme storms.

About 390,000 people live within 12 miles of the plant, including 120,000 children. Most of the residents within 3 miles of the plant are people of color and the poverty rate is 50% higher than the state average.

We are seeing increased respiratory and cardiovascular diseases in our offices. More children are missing school because they must stay home or even go to a hospital emergency room when air quality is bad. We advise our patients to check the local air quality index and wear masks to protect them from particulates, even when COVID-19 mandates end. We caution patients against working outdoors during heatwaves. The polluted air and associated medical problems in Waukegan cause huge costs for the community.
Also, we hear from our colleagues in obstetrics that they are seeing a rising number of preterm or low birth weight babies. These medical dangers are related to heat and bad air quality.
SBP: The clean energy legislation would phase out power plants in Illinois that burn coal or natural gas. It would create incentives for generating energy by wind and solar power systems, and for installing battery storage. As part of this transition, the Waukegan Generating Station would be shut down and there would be programs to redevelop the site and provide job training for the workers.

This legislation would transition Illinois from burning coal and natural gas to clean, renewable forms of energy. It would set deadlines for closing coal and natural gas power plants. This bill would promote better health in Illinois and Waukegan.

Our state can generate electricity in ways that do not make our residents sick and die prematurely. Our patients and the Waukegan community should not have to breathe polluted air or suffer from the heatwaves and floods associated with climate change.

State and federal environmental regulations implemented over the past twenty years reduced the fine particulate matter and mercury emitted by coal power plants. While these regulations helped the people of Waukegan, more should be done. Advances in wind, solar and battery technologies now allow for cost-effective replacement of these old, polluting power plants.

Importantly, the legislation would address the needs of communities like Waukegan where power plants would close through incentives to locate clean energy production and storage as well as training for jobs in energy efficiency and clean energy.

Also, we understand that the costs of generating electricity by wind and solar power systems are less than the costs of operating and maintaining old coal plants like Waukegan. Supplying clean, cheaper electricity will be good for Waukegan’s households and businesses.

Closing the powerplant is consistent with Waukegan’s new Sustainability Plan unanimously passed in 2021and the fits with a proposal for the new Comprehensive Plan passed in 2018, helping guide decisions related to economic development that include environmental impacts.
Please support rapid passage of clean energy legislation for Illinois.
